title: Cairo founded
hookLine: the Fatimids, an Isma'ili dynasty, found a new city beside the Nile

cards: Ropes are strung around a plain beside the Nile, hung with bells. Workers wait with their tools. Astrologers watch the sky for the right moment to begin, when they'll shake the ropes and the digging will start.
Then a crow lands on a rope. The bells ring. The workers dig.
And the planet rising at that moment, so the story goes, was the one Arabic astronomers called the victorious. That, people say, is how the city got its name: al-Qahira. In English, Cairo.

teach.b: Take the crow as a story people tell; the history behind it is sturdier. The Fatimids named themselves for Fatimah, daughter of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and wife of Ali, and they claimed descent from her.
They were Isma'ili Shi'i Muslims. Shi'i Muslims hold that leadership of the community passed to Ali, and then to imams among his and Fatimah's descendants.
The Isma'ilis followed one line of those imams, and the Fatimid caliphs said they were those imams.
That made a crowded sky of caliphs: one in Baghdad, a Fatimid caliph who had already claimed the title in North Africa, and the Cordoba caliph you met last week, who took it after them.

Sunnis and Shi'is understood that leadership differently, and still do. The Fatimids rose in North Africa, then took Egypt. Their general, Jawhar, laid out a new walled city for his caliph, al-Mu'izz.
An older city, Fustat, already stood nearby, built in the early years of Muslim rule in Egypt. The new city was a royal enclosure: palaces, a great mosque, walls with gates.
Much of ordinary life went on outside it, in Fustat.

Over the years the two grew into each other, until the name Cairo covered both. Today Isma'ili Muslims around the world count the Fatimid imams as part of their own story, and Cairo still keeps Fatimid gates and mosques.
A city built to announce a claim, then lived in by everyone.

how: Isma'ili Muslims today count the Fatimid imams as part of their own history, and Cairo's Fatimid gates and mosques are still visited and prayed in.

o: al-Qahira, the victorious: a royal city by the Nile
Fustat, the older city built when Muslims came to Egypt
a Baghdad caliph's new capital on the Tigris

games.q: who's who in the story — tap the pairs.
p: the general who laid out the city
the caliph the city was built for

s: Cairo was built on empty land with no city nearby
the older city of Fustat already stood beside it, and the two grew into one.
the Fatimid caliphs were Isma'ili Shi'i Muslims
they claimed to be the imams of the Isma'ili line, descended from Ali and Fatimah.
the crow and the bells are recorded fact
it's a story people tell about how the city got its name.

games.q: you're a worker beside the Nile. ropes with bells circle the plain, and the astrologers are still waiting for the right moment. a crow lands on a rope. what happens?
o: the bells ring, and the digging starts early.
games.why: in the story people tell, the bells ring and the digging begins, under the planet called the victorious, and the city takes the name al-Qahira.

practice: Picture the Nile running north, and on its east bank two cities side by side, an old busy one and a new walled one with palaces, slowly merging.

Now picture your own town the same way: where was the old center, where did newer neighborhoods grow, and who lives in them? If you pray, remember the people of your city; if you don't, hold them in mind with good will.

wordCard.voice: Cairo founded. The Fatimids, an Isma'ili dynasty, built a royal city beside the old Fustat, and named it al-Qahira, the victorious. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: al-Qahira, Cairo's name, usually given as the victorious.

carryVoice: Your line: the victorious city. Fatimid gates still stand among its streets. That's day nine hundred forty-six.
